Dijkstra

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch two extra lines show whether its two smaller copies leave a gap, fit exactly, or overlap.
How to play: Drag a blue dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show areas, color, hints or names, or try a shape button to jump to a triangle.
Look for the math

Move one corner of the triangle and the two small copies drawn from C change size. Which copy is bigger tells you whether the square on AB is bigger or smaller than the other two squares put together. That is Dijkstra's restatement of the Pythagorean theorem.

Two copies of the same triangle

Write the angles as alpha at A, beta at B and gamma at C, opposite the sides a = BC, b = CA and c = AB. The applet draws CL so that angle ACL = beta, and CN so that angle BCN = alpha. Because L and N sit on the line AB, both small triangles have the same three angles as ABC. They are similar triangles: ACL matches ABC with A→A, C→B, L→C, and BCN matches it with B→B, C→A, N→C. Press Hint to see the matching angles at C. The logic test checked both angle equalities and the side ratios in 1,360 non-degenerate triangles.

Compare the areas

All three triangles have the same height above the line AB, and the area of a triangle is half its base times its height. Similarity then gives one positive number k with

area(ACL) = k·b²,  area(BCN) = k·a²,  area(ABC) = k·c².

The striped rectangles in the applet have twice those areas, so the same comparison applies to both. The page prints area(ACL)/a² = area(BCN)/b², but the construction gives area(ACL)/b² = area(BCN)/a² = area(ABC)/c²: the page swaps those two numerators. The test found the printed version false whenever a and b differ. Adding the pieces hides the slip, so the page's final claim is still true:

sign(area(ACL) + area(BCN) − area(ABC)) = sign(a² + b² − c²).

Why the angles give the same sign

Since the three angles add to 180°, alpha + beta − gamma has the same sign as 90° − gamma. When gamma is obtuse the pieces leave a gap, as in the starting triangle; when it is exactly 90° they fit and CL and CN coincide at the foot H, giving the familiar square-on-the-hypotenuse picture; when it is acute the pieces overlap. The law of cosines says c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(gamma), hence a² + b² − c² = 2ab·cos(gamma) and its sign is the sign of 90° − gamma too. The logic test compared all three signs in 1,360 configurations — a lattice of positions for C plus 900 random triangles — including exact right triangles, and they agreed every time.

What changed from the applet

The four buttons stand for the applet's four checkboxes; Color is switched off and disabled unless Areas is on, just as the old panel enforced it. Here you drag the three corners (the Java applet also let you drag the whole triangle), and three shape buttons jump to a triangle with a gap, an exact fit or an overlap. The status line says in words what the picture shows. The original applet is Bogomolny's; the algebraic proof quoted on his page is credited to Guoping Zeng and was not transcribed here. This is an illustration: there is no win or loss, only a picture to explore.

Turn on Color, Names and Hint, then press Right at C. Watch L and N merge into H, then press a neighbouring shape button and see the pieces separate again.
